subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Brazil's Coffee Empire
description: A quick win: understand Brazil's Coffee Empire.

hook.text: Brazil didn't grow coffee before 1727. By 1850, it produced more than every other country combined.

buildup.text: Colonel Francisco de Melo Palheta obtained seeds from French Guiana through a diplomatic—and romantic—affair.

discovery.text: Brazil's vast, flat terrain and tropical climate were perfect. Coffee plantations exploded across São Paulo state.

twist.text: Brazilian coffee was built on slave labor. Over 1.5 million enslaved Africans worked the plantations by 1850.

climax.text: Brazil still produces about one-third of all coffee worldwide—a dominance over 170 years old.

punchline.text: Seeds from a love affair built a global empire.

quiz.question: Roughly what share of world coffee does Brazil still produce?

details.summary: Brazil became the world's largest coffee producer in the 1840s and has never relinquished the title. Coffee built railways, cities, and a wealthy planter class. It funded Brazil's industrialization and shaped its politics. Today Brazil produces about a third of all the world's coffee.
details.whyItMatters: Brazil's dominance made coffee a global commodity. Understanding Brazil's coffee history is essential to understanding both the country and the world coffee market.
takeaways: Brazil became the largest producer in the 1840s and still leads
Coffee funded Brazil's infrastructure and industrialization
Brazil produces roughly one-third of the world's coffee today

faq.question: How did Brazil come to dominate coffee production?
faq.answer: Brazil had ideal growing conditions, vast available land, and, until 1888, enslaved labor that kept costs extremely low. Government policy encouraged coffee expansion. European immigration after abolition provided more workers. Sheer scale and favorable geography made Brazil unbeatable.

faq.question: How does Brazil's production affect global coffee prices?
faq.answer: Brazil is so dominant that a single frost or drought there can spike global prices overnight. Its harvest season sets the tone for annual supply. Brazilian production decisions, from planting to export policy, ripple through the entire world coffee market.
